The healthcare Q&A matches provide different perspectives on predicting the severity of subclavian steal syndrome (SSS) using blood pressure differences between arms. While some studies suggest that brachial systolic blood pressure difference is related to the severity of SSS, others argue that it may not be a reliable predictor.

One study found that a greater blood pressure difference between arms was associated with more severe symptoms in patients with SSS. This suggests that the severity of steal might indeed be related to differences in blood pressure between arms.

However, another study concluded that brachial systolic blood pressure difference is not a good predictor of SSS severity. They noted that there were significant variations in BP readings across different measurements and interpretations of the data.

It's essential to consider multiple factors when assessing the severity of subclavian steal syndrome, including clinical symptoms, imaging findings, and other medical history. Blood pressure differences between arms are just one aspect to be taken into account, as they may not accurately reflect the overall condition of an individual.

In summary, while some studies suggest a possible relationship between blood pressure differences between arms and SSS severity, others indicate that this approach is not reliable. A comprehensive evaluation of patients with SSS should take into account multiple factors, including clinical symptoms, imaging findings, and other medical history to determine the best course of treatment.
